title: Dry vs Wet Volume: Bushels, Dry Quarts and the Trap
h1: Dry vs wet volume — bushel, dry pint, dry quart
description: 1 US dry quart = 1.101 L. 1 US liquid quart = 0.946 L. 16% difference. Grain sold in dry, milk in liquid — same word, different unit.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Dry measure and liquid measure use the same names (pint, quart) for different volumes.
body: US customary preserves two parallel volume systems for historical trade reasons. Dry volumes cover grain, produce, salt — anything measured heaped or level. Liquid volumes cover fluids. Modern practice usually specifies which system, but recipes and shipping manifests occasionally drop the qualifier.

> 1 US dry pint = 550.6 mL
> 1 US liquid pint = 473.2 mL (14% smaller)
> 1 US dry quart = 1101.2 mL
> 1 US bushel = 32 dry quarts = 35.24 L
> 1 US peck = 8 dry quarts = 8.81 L
Dry: grain (bushel of wheat = 27.22 kg by convention), produce shipping, some spices. Liquid: everything else. Berries — depending on state — sold in either.
'2 quarts flour' in a US colonial-recipe book means 2 dry quarts = 2.20 L. Modern cook reads as liquid quarts and uses 1.89 L — 15% shortfall by volume. Baking recipes shift dramatically at 15% off.
Same word, different volume. Dry ≈ 1.16 × liquid. Recipes and shipping manifests should always specify.

faqs.a: Volume by strict definition, but customary trade converts to mass by commodity (wheat bushel = 60 lb, corn = 56 lb).

faqs.q: Do metric systems have this split?
faqs.a: No — SI uses litres for both. The split is US customary only.
